claim: Replaying a $50,000, 10-year private loan over every 120-month window of 3-month T-bill history since 1954 (753 start months), a variable rate that starts at 7.5% and moves one-for-one with the bill rate ended up costing more in total interest than a 9% fixed rate in 14.2% of windows. The median window had the variable loan $3,832 cheaper (fixed-rate interest: $26,005). But the losses were concentrated: 28.4% of windows starting 1954-1980 cost more versus 3.5% starting 1981 or later, and the worst window (starting 1977-04) cost $11,219 more, with the variable rate peaking at 20.6%. History, not a forecast.

numbers.definition: Data: data/TB3MS.csv (FRED TB3MS, 3-Month Treasury Bill Secondary Market Rate, Discount Basis, monthly, percent), 1934-01 through 2026-08 (last value 3.72). Loan: $50,000, 120 monthly payments, interest = balance*rate/1200 each month; the payment is recomputed as the level payment over the remaining months whenever the rate changes (month k=0..119, remaining = 120-k). Fixed loan: 9.00% all 120 months. Variable loan for a start month s: rate_k = 3.78 + max(0, 3.72 + TB3MS[s+k] - TB3MS[s]) (3.72 = latest TB3MS, 3.78 = 7.50 - 3.72, so rate_0 = 7.50 and the index cannot go below zero), unrounded. Start months s: every month from 1954-01 through 2016-09 (last start with 120 months of data). Difference = total variable interest - total fixed interest over the 120 months. Number of start months.
Last start month with a full 120-month window (2016-09-01).

assumptions: Offers taken as given: 9.00% fixed and 7.50% variable at origination; the variable loan reprices monthly as a fixed margin plus the 3-month T-bill rate (proxy for the SOFR or similar index lenders use).
Index path = today's T-bill level (3.72) plus the historical change since the start month, floored at zero; no rate cap.
Repayment starts immediately, 120 level payments re-amortized when the rate changes; no in-school deferment, fees, autopay discounts, prepayment or default.
Start months 1954-01 onward (after the 1951 Treasury-Fed accord ended the wartime yield peg).
